title: KV cache eviction / paging / prefix reuse deep dive - Lucid Core
summary: SE-led deep dive on KV cache eviction/paging and prefix reuse for long-context workloads. Covered observed eviction patterns, paging thresholds, interaction with batching and quantization, VPC/network constraints, and next steps to run targeted benchmarks and share security docs.
next_steps: Redwood to share KV cache tuning guide and eviction dashboard screenshots
Lucid Core to run provided benchmark harness on sample workload and share logs
Send SOC2 + secops doc to Sophie
Schedule follow-up in 2 weeks to review benchmark results

transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2026-11-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Tom Wu (Redwood Product), Maya Chen (Lucid Core CTO), Amit Varma (Lucid Core ML), Sophie King (Lucid Core Security), Noah Patel (Lucid Core Infra)

[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Lena from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. Diego and Priya from our SE team are with me, and Tom from product to help on any product-level constraints. Maya, Amit, Sophie — thanks for making time. Quick agenda: dig into the KV cache eviction/paging behavior you've been seeing with long-context sessions, talk about prefix reuse impacts, and outline actionable tuning and benchmark steps.

[00:25] Maya: Yeah thanks. We've been seeing unexpected token regen and higher latency on sessions over ~8k tokens, and we suspect the KV cash — sorry, cache — is getting evicted and then we see paging. It's been causing spikes in tail latency which is killing the UX on our transcript viewer.

[00:47] Diego: Got it. Can you quickly confirm your stack — are you on Redwood Hosted or Dedicated, and are you using any of the quantized variants?

[00:59] Amit: We're on Redwood Dedicated in our VPC, GPU workers 8xA100-ish. We tried int8 quantization for memory savings on a few models. We also have batching enabled at the inference gateway with fairly aggressive group windowing to improve throughput.

[01:20] Priya: Ok that gives us useful signal — Dedicated + VPC means we can look at both kernel selection and instance memory pressure. Two likely vectors: KV cache memory pressure causing eviction, and when the runtime attempts to serve a long context it pages keys back which costs latency. Quantization can change memory layout which affects how much KV fits in GPU DRAM vs host pinned memory.

[01:45] Sophie: From security side we also need to understand data residency for the KV cache and whether any paging moves things to host memory or disk — and what encryption protections remain.

[02:03] Tom: Quick note — paging here refers to runtime-level spill from GPU RAM to host or NVMe staging in extreme cases; it's not OS swap in your VPC. But it does add tens to hundreds of ms per token depending on bandwidth.

[02:22] Amit: When we repro, we see a pattern: after sustained multi-session traffic, eviction counter bumps, and then a few sessions with 12k+ tokens suffer 200–400ms tail increases. Also we've seen prefix reuse across sessions where earlier conversation prefixes are similar but not identical.

[02:45] Diego: Okay that's the classic prefix-reuse and eviction interplay. If prefixes are similar but with small differences, KV keys may not be reused and you lose the benefit of the cache. Also if you have aggressive batching, the runtime might group requests in a way that forces larger KV footprints concurrently.

[03:10] Maya: Can you show what metrics we should look at? Our dashboard has some eviction_count and cache_hit_rate, but not sure which thresholds are meaningful.

[03:23] Diego: Sure — high level you want to monitor: KV_cache_size_bytes (per model shard), eviction_rate (evictions/min), avg_prefix_kv_slots_used, cache_hit_ratio_by_prefix_length, and gpu_mem_free_pct. For paging, look at page_in_latency and page_in_throughput and any host_io spikes. If eviction_rate > ~0.1 evictions/min on sustained load, or cache_hit_ratio drops below ~85% for long contexts, that's a red flag.

[03:58] Priya: Also watch for sudden spikes in cpu-side stall or long batch formation windows — these often correlate with when the runtime is refilling KV caches from host.

[04:12] Noah: A question on quantization — we used int8 to reduce model size. Are you saying int8 can affect KV cache behavior?

[04:22] Tom: Yes — quantization changes memory density and layout. For some kernels we keep KV in packed formats that are better or worse for eviction locality. In tests, int8 reduced model weights by ~30–40% but KV footprint reduction varied by model and sequence length. So it's not guaranteed.

[04:45] Amit: Hmm. So we shouldn't assume quantization always buys more KV headroom.

[04:50] Diego: Right. We recommend measuring KV bytes per active token for your actual sequence distribution. We can provide a small harness that emulates your session mix and returns per-step KV usage and eviction traces.

[05:05] Maya: That would be helpful. Also about prefix reuse — is there runtime support for prefix canonicalization to increase reuse?

[05:15] Priya: We do have heuristics. Runtime can hash prefixes with normalization options — trimming whitespace, lowercasing, or canonicalizing entities — but there are tradeoffs because normalization may change model outputs. For multi-tenant dedicated setups we can surface a prefix-reuse score and you can choose to enable best-effort canonicalization.

[05:42] Sophie: From security, any normalization means we need to be careful about PII handling if normalization stores intermediate data. Does Redwood encrypt cache at rest and in transit?

[05:55] Lena: Good question. For Dedicated in VPC, the KV cache lives in GPU memory primarily; if the runtime spills to host or NVMe, those pages are encrypted using the customer-managed KMS when configured and are stored in the instance ephemeral storage — we can provide architecture diagrams. We'll share SOC2 artifacts and our KMS integration notes as a follow-up.

[06:18] Maya: Perfect. Back to the eviction: what's the most common root cause you see — real memory pressure vs fragmentation vs pathological prefixes?

[06:29] Diego: Usually a mix. Common causes: (1) underprovisioned GPU memory for your working set (esp with many concurrent sessions), (2) batching patterns that increase concurrent KV footprint, (3) quantization/incompatible kernel causing larger-than-expected KV layout, (4) prefix churn where lots of slightly different prefixes defeat reuse, and (5) long-lived sessions with growing context without proactive trimming.

[06:57] Amit: On (1) we think we have spare capacity but might be misreading free memory because fragmentation isn't visible from the OS. Any tools to surface fragmentation?

[07:07] Priya: We surface a fragmentation metric in the RD dashboard (fragmentation_pct) — we'll send screenshots. Fragmentation often looks like low usable contiguous memory despite overall free bytes. It shows as elevated allocation failures when the runtime tries to create large KV tensors.

[07:24] Maya: Can we tune eviction policy parameters? We saw a default LRU-ish strategy but maybe TTLs?

[07:33] Diego: Yes. There are tunables: eviction_policy (LRU, LFU, tiered), eviction_threshold_pct (what percent free triggers eviction), and prefix_pin_ratio (fraction of prefix slots reserved for recent popular prefixes). For long-context workloads we often set eviction_threshold higher and pin hot prefixes. But pinning increases reserved memory and could worsen fragmentation, so it's a balance.

[07:59] Sophie: If we pin prefixes, do we risk exposing more data? What's the retention?

[08:07] Tom: Pinning is an in-memory policy; retention is controllable and respects your data retention settings. No pinned data is persisted beyond the instance lifecycle unless you enable persistent caching. We'll document defaults.

[08:20] Lena: Let's walk through a concrete repro you provided earlier — Amit, you shared a log sample where eviction_count spikes at minute 23 of a load test. Can you describe the load pattern?

[08:33] Amit: Sure — traffic is a mix: 60% short support-like queries (~300 tokens), 30% medium (~2k tokens), 10% long conversations that grow to ~14k tokens. Concurrency peaks at ~120 QPS with batching window 25ms. Eviction spike happened after ~20 minutes steady state.

[08:53] Diego: That concurrency with batching window will create overlapping KV footprints. For example, long sessions will keep their KV plus medium sessions' KV concurrently before old entries age out. With a 25ms batch window at 120 QPS, you're effectively pulling in a lot of simultaneous contexts.

[09:10] Priya: Two immediate suggestions: (A) try reducing batching window to 10–15ms for long-context routes so you reduce concurrent KV breadth, and (B) carve a dedicated pool for long-context sessions with higher memory headroom so they don't evict each other's prefixes.

[09:26] Maya: Carving dedicated pool — is that something we can do with Redwood Dedicated?

[09:32] Lena: Yes, with Dedicated you can configure GPU pools and routing policies — route long-context endpoints to a pool with larger instance types or fewer concurrent slots. We can propose a config. We'll also highlight cost tradeoffs.

[09:44] Noah: On mailbox: we saw page_in_latency metrics spike around the same time. Is that consistent with spills?

[09:50] Diego: Yes page_in_latency correlates with spill-in of KV pages from host or NVMe. If you see page_in_throughput saturate network or host io, you'll get the latency spike. Two mitigations: increase on-GPU memory by larger instances or reduce concurrent KV by routing/buffering, and tune spill to NVMe with higher bandwidth.

[10:12] Amit: Any quick experiments we can run to isolate whether fragmentation or insufficient total memory is the issue?

[10:19] Priya: One experiment: run a staged load where you slowly ramp concurrent long sessions while keeping short sessions off, then ramp short sessions and compare eviction behavior. If eviction starts during the long-session ramp it's total headroom; if it starts when shorts ramp, it's concurrent breadth. Also run the allocation trace we provide to see allocation failures vs evictions.

[10:40] Sophie: For security sign-off we need to confirm that the runtime never writes unencrypted KV pages to customer S3 or external storage unless explicitly enabled.

[10:50] Tom: Correct — by default nothing is persisted externally. Spills are ephemeral and encrypted; we'll include docs.

[11:00] Diego: Another point on prefix reuse: if your app attaches variable metadata or timestamps to every user message, that will defeat reuse. Consider normalizing out stable context and only send variable fields as separate tokens or via metadata that doesn't enter the LM prefix.

[11:16] Maya: That may require architecture changes but sounds worthwhile. We also have some internal heuristics that append session IDs to every message for debugging — maybe that's the culprit.

[11:27] Lena: Small wins we often see: strip stable prefixes from user messages, enable prefix canonicalization heuristics on hot routes, and carve long-context pools. For bigger wins: dedicated longer-GPU instances and targeted pinning for a small set of hot prefixes.

[11:45] Amit: What about model selection? Are some models more KV friendly?

[11:50] Tom: Yes — model architecture and attention implementation matter. Some transformer variants produce smaller KV per token. We'll share model-specific profiles in the tuning guide. Also certain kernels we ship for longer context are more memory efficient.

[12:04] Maya: Can we run a comparative benchmark using our trace on Redwood infra? We can give a small sample workload and you can run it to see eviction/paging behavior across instance types.

[12:14] Diego: Absolutely — we'll run a controlled benchmark. We'll need your sample trace, request distribution, sequence distribution, and any normalization rules. We'll return per-token latency, eviction traces, page_in metrics, fragmentation profile.

[12:27] Lena: I'll follow up with the benchmark harness and the config template to capture your traffic pattern. Diego will include recommended dashboard charts.

[12:35] Sophie: For compliance, please include the KMS integration steps and a note on who has access to ephemeral keys in Dedicated.

[12:44] Tom: We'll include a short note and a diagram.

[12:50] Amit: Quick technical question — how does batching interact with KV cache warm-up? If we put multiple requests in a batch, does that pre-warm KV for later steps?

[12:59] Priya: Batching increases concurrency which can both help and hurt. It can amortize compute per token but increases the number of distinct KV sets held concurrently. It doesn't pre-warm for later unrelated sessions; warm-up is per prefix hash. If the batch contains multiple requests with overlapping prefixes, you will see reuse, but if they are disjoint you increase KV load.

[13:23] Maya: Noted. On prioritization — what's the low-effort change we should try first?

[13:29] Diego: Reduce batching window for long-context routes and enable prefix canonicalization with conservative normalization. Those are low-risk. Then run the ramp experiments.

[13:40] Lena: Ok let's recap next steps — Diego provides benchmark harness and recommended dashboard charts; Priya will share eviction/pinning tunables documentation and screenshots; I will send pricing/bench spreadsheet and security pack; Lucid Core will run the benchmark and share logs; Sophie will review security docs. Schedule follow-up in two weeks.

[13:58] Maya: Sounds good. Any blockers?

[14:02] Lena: Not from our side. Anything else from Lucid Core?

[14:06] Amit: Just one thing — we'd love to see an example of a configuration that pins the top 20 prefixes and routes long sessions to a dedicated pool — a config snippet would be helpful.

[14:15] Diego: We'll include that in the doc pack.

[14:20] Sophie: And SOC2 artifact + KMS steps.

[14:24] Lena: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts noted.

[14:30] --- End of call transcript (truncated) ---

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings ("KV cash"), speaker overlaps, timestamps approximate.
